questions.lead_in: What monitoring parameters would need to be conducted on a routine basis?
questions.explanation: Electrocardiogram Azithromycin can cause QTc prolongation, especially if it is concomitantly prescribed with another QTc prolonging agent. Thus an electrocardiogram (ECG) should be routinely monitored.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman was evaluated for nausea, anorexia, and fatigue. She underwent deceased donor kidney transplantation 6 months prior and had normal renal function with an appropriate tacrolimus level at her last follow-up. Her current medications were tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She reported that she took some leftover clarithromycin 5 days ago for what she thought was a tooth infection. Her vitals and physical examination were normal. Investigations: Serum creatinine 4.0 mg/dL Urinalysis normal
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?
questions.explanation: Tacrolimus toxicity Macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin and clarithromycin, and azoles such as posaconazole and fluconazole can decrease the metabolism of cyclosporine and tacrolimus leading to markedly increased levels and toxicity. Physicians and patients should be aware of interactions among antibiotics and immunosuppressive medications.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q25

questions.question: A patient has Streptococcus pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia with the following MICs: penicillin 2, erythromycin 64, clindamycin 256.
questions.question_raw: Strep pneumonia CAP with MICs as follows: Pen 2; Erythro 64; Clinda 256

parts.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance in pneumococcus?
What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
What type is present here?

parts_raw.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
B.  What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?
C. What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
d) What type is present here?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes, for this non-CNS infection treated parenterally. Current breakpoints define a pneumococcus as penicillin-susceptible if the MIC is <=2 ug/mL for non-CNS parenteral therapy, so an MIC of 2 is susceptible IV. (It would be intermediate/resistant by the oral non-CNS breakpoint of <=0.06 and resistant by the CNS breakpoint of <=0.06, so it could not be used orally or for meningitis.)
b) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs): mutations in the genes encoding PBPs (notably PBP2b for low-level and PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) reduce penicillin's binding affinity. These altered genes are acquired by transformation (e.g., from S. mitis).
c) (1) Ribosomal target methylation encoded by ermB (methylates A2058 in domain V of 23S rRNA), giving high-level resistance (>=64 ug/mL) and the MLSB phenotype. (2) Efflux encoded by mefA, giving lower-level resistance (usually <=16 ug/mL), affecting macrolides only.
d) MLSB (ermB-mediated ribosomal methylation): resistance to both the macrolide (erythromycin 64) and clindamycin (256) indicates ribosomal methylation, not an efflux pump (which would spare clindamycin).

cohort_answer.text:
IV Non-meningitic: ≤2 is susceptible --- can use; Po pen: ≤0.06 µg/mL (same breakpoints as meningitis); Meningitic: pen susceptible is ≤0.06 µg/mL, resistant is ≥0.12 µg/mL
Alteration of target enzymes (PBPs)
Efflux pumps (mef in strep pneumo, mSRA in staph aureus), resistance to macrolides, not clinda (M phenotype); Target site alteration by methylation of ribosome to prevent drug binding, resistance to both macrolides, lincosamides, streptogamins (MLSB)
Target site alteration MLSB

questions.question: Clindamycin.
questions.question_raw: Clindamycin:

parts.text: Why doesn't this drug work in gram-negatives?
When do you need a D-test?

parts_raw.text: Why doesn't this drug work in gram negatives?
When do you need a D-test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Enterobacteriaceae (and Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter spp.) are intrinsically resistant because of poor permeability of the cellular outer envelope to the drug, so clindamycin cannot reach its 50S ribosomal target.
b) Perform a D-test (erythromycin-clindamycin double-disk diffusion) when clindamycin is being considered to treat a Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes isolate that is macrolide/erythromycin-resistant but appears clindamycin-susceptible in vitro; a positive test (blunting of the clindamycin zone toward the erythromycin disk) indicates inducible MLSB resistance and predicts emergence of clindamycin resistance on treatment.

cohort_answer.text: Doesn't work in GNR: Clinda doesn't permeate the cellular outer membrane well. D-test needed: When the isolate is resistant to erythromycin but sensitive to clindamycin

parts.text: What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance?
Can penicillin be used here?

Which mechanism is in play here?

Can pen be used here?

questions.model_answer:
a) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) with reduced affinity for penicillin, due to mutations in PBP genes (PBP2b for low-level, PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) acquired by transformation.
b) Yes, if given IV for this non-CNS infection: MIC <=2 ug/mL is susceptible by the non-CNS parenteral breakpoint. It could not be used orally (oral non-CNS susceptible <=0.06) or for CNS infection.
c) Two mechanisms: ermB-encoded ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA (high-level resistance >=64, MLSB phenotype) and mefA-encoded efflux pump (lower-level resistance <=16, macrolides only).
d) MLSB (ermB ribosomal methylation): high-level resistance to both erythromycin AND clindamycin indicates methylation rather than an efflux pump.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin: Mechanism of resistance: altered enzyme structure (PBP) with reduced affinity for the antibiotic. Can be used if IV completely (MIC ≤2). If oral (or CNS infection), cannot use it. Macrolides and Clindamycin: Most likely mechanism is ermB (methylation of ribosome binding site). This gives high level resistance to macrolides and clindamycin (MLSB phenotype). Another mechanism of resistance is mefA (efflux pump), which is low level resistance, but this does not generally impact clindamycin

questions.question: Clindamycin: mechanism of action, tissue penetration, and inducible resistance testing.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action of clindamycin?
Name one organ system clindamycin cannot penetrate.
Name four organisms that should be tested for inducible clindamycin resistance (ermA, ermC).
When should you test for inducible resistance?
Why are gram-negatives intrinsically resistant?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action of clindamycin?
Name one organ system clindamycin cannot penetrate.
Name four organisms that should be tested for inducible clindamycin resistance (ermA, ermC).
When should you test for inducible resistance?
Why are Gram negatives intrinsically resistant?

questions.model_answer:
a) Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA, overlapping the macrolide/chloramphenicol site) and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, chiefly by interfering with the transpeptidation reaction in early chain elongation.
b) The central nervous system — clindamycin achieves only clinically insignificant CSF concentrations even with inflamed meninges, so it should not be used for CNS infection.
c) (1) Staphylococcus aureus; (2) Streptococcus pyogenes; (3) Streptococcus agalactiae (group B Streptococcus); (4) Streptococcus pneumoniae (beta-hemolytic streptococci generally).
d) When the isolate is macrolide/erythromycin-resistant but appears clindamycin-susceptible in vitro — do the erythromycin-clindamycin D-test; a positive result indicates inducible MLSB resistance and predicts clindamycin failure.
e) Enterobacteriaceae (and Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter) show poor permeability of the outer envelope to clindamycin, so the drug cannot reach the ribosome.

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Inhibition of protein production by binding to the 50s ribosome portion (50s: Macrolides, clindamycin, Linezolid; 30s: Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines). Cannot penetrate: CNS. Test for inducible resistance: S. aureus, Strep. pneumoniae, Beta-hemolytic Strep, Strep. agalactiae. When to test: when macrolides are I/R but clindamycin listed as S (routinely screened on automated systems). GNB intrinsic resistance: poor permeability of outer membrane to the drug

parts_raw.text: Fill in the chart on macrolide resistance mechanisms

questions.model_answer:
Background: macrolides bind a pocket of the 23S subunit of the 50S ribosome at domain V of the peptidyl transferase loop, blocking protein assembly.
(1) Ribosomal target methylation - gene ermB - methylates base A2058 in domain V of 23S rRNA, altering the pocket; high-level resistance (>=64 ug/mL); MLSB phenotype, so it DOES include clindamycin (plus lincosamides and streptogramin B).
(2) Efflux pump - gene mefA - extrudes the macrolide; lower-level resistance (usually <=16 ug/mL); affects macrolides ONLY, does NOT include clindamycin.

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides insert into a pocket of the 23S subunit of the 50S ribosome, attaching at domain V of the peptidyl transferase loop, blocking protein assembly. mefA-encoded efflux pumps: pump that extrudes macrolides, low level resistance MIC<16, affects macrolide resistance only. ermB-encoded methylases: alter the ribosomal binding site, high level resistance MIC>64, MLSB phenotype - inducible resistance to Macrolide/Lincosamide/Streptogramin B (includes clindamycin).

questions.model_answer:
a) Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA, overlapping macrolide binding site) and inhibits protein synthesis by interfering with transpeptidation in early chain elongation; it also suppresses toxin/virulence-protein production (advantageous in streptococcal toxic shock and necrotizing infection).

questions.question_raw: Q59 (2003 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance

parts.text: What is the percentage of clindamycin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus?
What is the mechanism of clindamycin resistance?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the % resistance to clindamycin in S. aureus?
b) What is the mechanism of clindamycin resistance?

questions.model_answer: a) Roughly 5% in community-acquired MRSA (mostly inducible), but constitutive MLSB resistance exceeds 90% in health care-associated MRSA. b) MLSB resistance: erm-encoded methylation of an adenine in the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, altering the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B binding site; may be inducible (D-test positive) or constitutive. Lincosamides are not subject to the macrolide efflux pumps (msrA/mef).

cohort_answer.text: a) ~5% for MSSA, 25% for MRSA. b) Alteration in 23S rRNA of 50S ribosomal subunit via methylation of adenine (modified binding site for ribosome inhibitors), usually plasmid mediated ('MLS type of resistance', seen in S. aureus, S. pyogenes, B. fragilis; encoded by ermA or ermC genes in S. aureus, can be inducible or constitutive). Also: mutations in ribosomal RNA/50S ribosomal proteins; inactivation of drug by plasmid-mediated 3-lincomycin 4-clindamycin O-nucleotidyltransferase in some staph/bacteroides species. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter spp. intrinsically resistant due to poor outer membrane permeability.

questions.model_answer: 1) Fluconazole over caspofungin (fluconazole achieves high urinary/renal and CSF levels; echinocandins have negligible urinary penetration). 2) Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline is not used to treat CDI and carries low risk of inducing CDI). 3) Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir/ganciclovir has potent anti-CMV activity; valacyclovir is poorly active against CMV). 4) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems interact with anti-epileptics, lowering levels, so the non-carbapenem beta-lactam is preferred). 5) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (per exam key, for a CNS bacterial infection; ampicillin over cloxacillin is also defensible for Listeria meningitis). 6) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
questions.beyond_mandell: Antibacterial/antifungal pairings draw on general ID pharmacology/guidance rather than this antiviral chapter; only the CMV/herpesvirus activity claims are grounded in Mandell Ch. 46.

cohort_answer.text:
Acyclovir over valacyclovir: HSV meningitis/encephalitis.
Valganciclovir over valacyclovir: Herpes B treatment better activity, CMV treatment.
Famciclovir over acyclovir: Uncomplicated zoster (famciclovir higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir, dosed TID rather than 5 times daily).
Atovaquone over dapsone: G6PD deficiency, Toxoplasmosis.
Doxycycline over TMP-SMX: Someone on Ramipril and Spironolactone with MRSA infection may want Doxycycline over TMP/SMX given risk of hyperkalemia.
Fluconazole over caspofungin: Cryptococcus not covered by echinocandins, urinary or CNS infections.
Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate: CNS infections, disseminated histoplasmosis, suspected mucormycosis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem: Enterococcus.
Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin: Anaerobic activity is best with moxi.
Metronidazole over clindamycin: Bacteroides fragilis, increasing clinda resistance.
Azithromycin over clarithromycin: Better for gram-negatives, esp. M catarrhalis and H flu.
Ampicillin over cloxacillin: Enterococci, Listeria.
Cefazolin over cloxacillin: Surgical prophylaxis, penicillin allergy, AIN, heart failure.

questions.model_answer: (1) Target-site modification: methylation of the 23S rRNA (domain V, adenine A2058) by a ribosomal methylase, reducing binding of macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B (MLS-B phenotype); gene = erm (ermB in S. pneumoniae, ermB/ermTR/ermA in GAS); clindamycin resistance = YES (constitutive MLS-B) - may be inducible and detected by D-test. (2) Active efflux: an ATP-driven/major-facilitator efflux pump exports 14- and 15-membered macrolides only (M phenotype), sparing 16-membered macrolides, clindamycin and streptogramins; gene = mef (mefA/mefE in S. pneumoniae, mefA in GAS); clindamycin resistance = NO.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) — associated with QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors or other QT-prolonging drugs; (2) Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, levofloxacin).

questions.question: What is the mechanism of resistance for each of the following?
questions.question_raw: What is the mechanism of resistance for the following:

parts.text: Vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VISA)
Fluoroquinolones in Streptococcus pneumoniae
Penicillin in Enterococcus faecium
Group A Streptococcus and erythromycin

parts_raw.text: VISA
FQ in Strep. pneumoniae
Penicillin in E. faecium
GAS & erythro

questions.model_answer: a) VISA: cell-wall changes (no enterococcal van genes) - a thickened cell wall whose excess D-Ala-D-Ala termini trap vancomycin in the outer peptidoglycan layers ('decoy'/clogging), plus increased cell-wall turnover, decreased autolytic activity, increased positive cell-wall charge, and reduced Agr function (mediated by mutations in TCSs such as GraSR, VraSR, WalKR). b) Fluoroquinolones in S. pneumoniae: stepwise target mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), plus efflux (PmrA). c) Penicillin/ampicillin in E. faecium: low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 - overexpression and/or mutation reducing beta-lactam binding. d) GAS + erythromycin: (1) erm-mediated ribosomal target methylation (23S rRNA) giving the MLSB phenotype and (2) mef-mediated macrolide efflux pump.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the VISA mechanism is in the slice (pp. 378-379); the S. pneumoniae fluoroquinolone, E. faecium PBP5, and GAS erm/mef mechanisms are from established Mandell/antimicrobial resistance knowledge (other chapters).

cohort_answer.text: VISA: Increased cell wall turnover. Increased thickness of cell wall and cross linking of peptidoglycan. S. pneumo with moxifloxacin - DNA gyrase, Topoisomerase IV. GAS with erythromycin - Erm gene - methylation of target site (MLSB phenotype); mef gene - efflux pump. E. faecium w/ penicillin: altered PBP5 - Overexpression

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.

parts_raw.text: For the following antibiotics, provide the mechanism of interaction with tacrolimus: Cipro, Vori, Rifampin, Clarithromycin

questions.model_answer: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate, so interactions reflect each drug's effect on CYP3A4. (1) Ciprofloxacin - weak/negligible CYP3A4 inhibition; little clinically significant effect on tacrolimus (monitor). (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; markedly increases tacrolimus levels (tacrolimus dose reduction required). (3) Rifampin - potent inducer of hepatic/intestinal CYP3A4, decreasing tacrolimus AUC/levels and risking acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least enzyme induction) is preferred in transplant recipients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology (Mandell rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin/tacrolimus interaction and rifabutin as preferred alternative).

cohort_answer.text: Ciprofloxacin: no clear known interaction (immunologic effects postulated, unlikely clinically relevant). Voriconazole: likely inhibition of CYP3A4 leading to increased tacrolimus levels. Rifampin: suspected induction of CYP3A4 leading to decreased tacrolimus levels. Clarithromycin: strong CYP3A4 inhibition leading to increased tacrolimus levels.

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance: state the resistance mechanism and suggested treatment for each of macrolides (and explain the D test), beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems.
questions.question_raw: Q53 (2007). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism for each, as well as suggested treatment: Macrolides (+ explain D test); Beta-lactamases; Pseudomonas and carbapenems

parts.text: State the mechanisms and treatments for each category (macrolides with the D test, beta-lactamases, and Pseudomonas with carbapenems).

parts_raw.text: State mechanisms and treatments for each category

questions.model_answer: a) Macrolides: (mechanisms) efflux via mef genes (low-level, MIC <=16) and ribosomal methylation via erm genes (high-level, MIC >=64). D test: an erythromycin disk placed near a clindamycin disk; blunting/flattening of the clindamycin zone on the side facing erythromycin (D-shaped zone) indicates inducible erm-mediated clindamycin resistance, so clindamycin should not be used. Treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for susceptible gram-positive cocci. Beta-lactamases: enzymatic hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring (penicillinases, ESBLs, AmpC cephalosporinases, carbapenemases); treat by adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor, using a stable agent (carbapenem for ESBL), or switching classes for carbapenemase producers. Pseudomonas and carbapenems: (1) loss of OprD porin (chiefly imipenem), (2) upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM, chiefly meropenem), and (3) acquired carbapenemases (metallo-beta-lactamases VIM/IMP/NDM, KPC, GES); treat per susceptibilities with an alternative active agent (e.g., ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam for non-MBL producers).
questions.beyond_mandell: Macrolide resistance mechanisms (mef/erm) and the D test are not covered in this Pseudomonas chapter; that content rests on general antimicrobial-resistance knowledge (Mandell resistance chapters/CLSI).

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides: efflux (mefA gene, lower level resistance MIC<=16); ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, high level MIC>=64). D test checks for inducible clindamycin resistance via inducible erm gene - blunting of zone of inhibition around clindamycin proximal to erythromycin disk (D-shaped zone = positive, indicates induced clindamycin resistance); suggested treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for GPC, septra for MRSA. Beta-lactamases: bacteria produce enzymes breaking down beta-lactam (penicillinase, cephalosporinase/ESBL, carbapenemase); treatment depends on spectrum - use cephalosporin/aztreonam/carbapenem, add beta-lactamase inhibitor, or switch classes (tigecycline, colistin). Pseudomonas and carbapenems: porin loss (OprD deficiency confers high resistance esp to imipenem); efflux pump; carbapenemase.

questions.question: Group A streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
questions.question_raw:
Q11 (2004 AM)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock

parts.text: List the antibiotics that are used and give the rationale for their use.

parts_raw.text: C) List the antibiotics that are used and give rationale for their use

questions.model_answer: High-dose penicillin PLUS clindamycin. Rationale: (1) Penicillin — all strains of GAS remain susceptible to it, giving reliable bactericidal killing. (2) Clindamycin — a protein-synthesis inhibitor that suppresses production of streptococcal exotoxins and M protein, and its efficacy is not reduced by large inoculum or stationary-phase growth (overcoming the “Eagle effect,” in which penicillin is less effective at high organism density). Clindamycin also dampens host cytokine production. Penicillin is added because clindamycin is bacteriostatic and rare clindamycin resistance can occur.
questions.beyond_mandell: The Eagle-effect/inoculum rationale for clindamycin is established Mandell teaching; the antibiotic combination and toxin-suppression rationale are grounded in the cited page.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin - all strains of GAS susceptible to penicillin; less effective during stationary growth phase (Eagle effect). Clindamycin - suppresses exotoxin and protein M production at ribosome; suppresses cytokine production by human mononuclear cells (also: Penicillin - bactericidal effect; Clindamycin - bacteriostatic anti-toxinic effect + inoculum effect)

questions.question: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the following: ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, rifampin, clarithromycin.
questions.question_raw: Interactions of tacrolimus with: Ciprofloxacin, Voriconazole, Rifampin, Clarithromycin.

parts.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

parts_raw.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

questions.model_answer: (1) Ciprofloxacin - only weak CYP3A4 inhibition; minimal clinically important change in tacrolimus. (2) Voriconazole - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; substantially increases tacrolimus levels, requiring dose reduction. (3) Rifampin - potent CYP3A4/intestinal enzyme inducer; decreases tacrolimus AUC and levels, risking subtherapeutic immunosuppression and acute graft rejection; rifabutin (least CYP3A4 induction) is the preferred rifamycin in transplant patients. (4) Clarithromycin - potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases tacrolimus levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin, voriconazole and clarithromycin mechanisms are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter covers only the rifampin interaction and rifabutin as the preferred transplant alternative.

cohort_answer.text: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate. Ciprofloxacin - weakly inhibits CYP3A4, may increase tacrolimus. Voriconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus levels (strongest contraindication; rifabutin should be used instead of rifampin to avoid interaction and reduce risk of acute graft rejection). Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreasing tacrolimus levels (risk of rejection). (2) Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increasing tacrolimus levels. (3) Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increasing tacrolimus levels.
b) (1) Gentamicin + tacrolimus - no true CYP-mediated interaction, but additive nephrotoxicity (both cause renal injury/acute kidney injury). (2) Mycophenolate mofetil + TMP-SMX - no true CYP interaction, but additive myelosuppression (leukopenia/cytopenias).
questions.beyond_mandell: Clarithromycin and fluconazole mechanisms and both additive-toxicity combinations are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter grounds only the rifampin-tacrolimus induction effect.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus. Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Gentamicin + tacrolimus: no true drug-drug interaction, but both can cause nephrotoxicity. MMF + TMP/SMX: no true DDI, both can cause myelosuppression.

questions.model_answer:
a) Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumophila) - anti-TNF-alpha therapy is a recognized risk factor, and pneumonia failing a beta-lactam with hyponatremia is classic.
b) (1) Urine antigen - Limitation: detects essentially only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so a negative test does not exclude other serogroups/species. (2) Lower respiratory culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract - Limitation: requires special media and expertise, is insensitive, and yield drops once antibiotics are started.
c) (1) Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin). (2) Fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin).
d) Doxycycline (a tetracycline).

cohort_answer.text: Legionella pneumophila. TNF-alpha inhibitors increase risk of intracellular pathogens (2-4 fold increase in TB and other granulomatous conditions; also Listeria, Legionella, Salmonella, HBV, VZV, JC virus, possible NTM/Nocardia, case reports of Crypto/Histo/Cocci). Tests: Urine legionella antigen (only detects serogroup 1) and culture (needs specialized charcoal-containing media); can also do DFA. Treatment classes: fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin), macrolides (azithromycin). Alternative: doxycycline.

parts.text: Two antibiotics causing QTc prolongation
One antiparasitic causing QTc prolongation
One anti-tuberculous drug causing QTc prolongation

parts_raw.text: 2 antibiotics causing QTc prolongation
1 antiparasitic causing QTc prolongation
1 anti-TB drug causing QTc prolongation

questions.model_answer:
a) Two antibiotics: (1) A fluoroquinolone — moxifloxacin (greatest QT effect; ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin less so) — blocks cardiac potassium channels, delays repolarization, and can precipitate torsades de pointes. (2) A macrolide — erythromycin (or azithromycin), also a QT-prolonging agent with which quinolone effects are additive.
b) One antiparasitic: quinine (alternatively chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine or mefloquine).
c) One anti-TB drug: bedaquiline (alternatively clofazimine).
questions.beyond_mandell: The quinolone chapter grounds only the antibiotics (fluoroquinolone and erythromycin/macrolide) for QT prolongation; the antiparasitic (quinine/chloroquine) and anti-TB (bedaquiline/clofazimine) agents are established QT-prolongers from general pharmacology/drug-safety references, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Antibiotics: Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin. Antiparasitic: Quinine, Sodium stibogluconate, Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (also possible but rare ~5%). Anti-TB: Clofazimine, Bedaquiline, Linezolid.

questions.question: Streptococcus pyogenes testing for erythromycin resistance.
questions.question_raw: Strep pyogenes testing for erythromycin resistance.

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of erythromycin (macrolide) resistance in Streptococcus pyogenes.
The isolate demonstrates clindamycin susceptibility. What test do you have to do to confirm this?

parts_raw.text: Name 2 mechanisms (1)
It demonstrates clindamycin susceptibility. What test do you have to do to confirm this (0.5)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ribosomal target-site modification: methylation of the 23S rRNA by an erm gene (erm(B)/erm(A)/erm(TR)), producing the MLSB phenotype (macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B cross-resistance), which may be constitutive or inducible. (2) Active efflux: a mef gene (mef(A))-encoded macrolide efflux pump conferring the M phenotype (macrolide resistance with retained clindamycin susceptibility).
b) Inducible clindamycin resistance testing by the D-zone test (double-disk diffusion, erythromycin disk adjacent to clindamycin disk). It is performed on isolates that are erythromycin-resistant but clindamycin-susceptible; blunting of the clindamycin zone toward the erythromycin disk (a D shape) indicates inducible erm-mediated MLSB resistance and predicts clindamycin failure.
questions.beyond_mandell: This Mandell chapter documents macrolide resistance rates but does not detail the resistance mechanisms or the D-zone test; the mechanisms and inducible-clindamycin (D-test) methodology are from standard CLSI/clinical microbiology guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms: Alteration in the ribosomal target site or efflux pumps (Mandell's) - mefA efflux pump (specific to strep, other names for staph); MLSB (macrolide lincosamide streptogramin B) resistance from ribosomal methylation altering ribosomal binding site, can be constitutive or inducible (induced by erythromycin exposure making resistant to clindamycin via inducible erm gene). Test: Do inducible clindamycin resistance testing (D-zone test) - only used for Staph species, S. pneumoniae, and beta-hemolytic streptococci; only performed in isolates erythromycin resistant and clindamycin susceptible; detects erm gene-mediated resistance (ribosomal methylation); confers MLSB phenotype
